name: Chapter 14: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
description: Energy bands, intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-n junction, diode, rectifiers, plus Zener, LED, transistor and logic gates

cards.term: Before transistors (1948), which devices controlled electron flow?
cards.definition: Vacuum tubes (valves): diode (2 electrodes), triode (cathode, plate, grid), tetrode, pentode

cards.term: Why were vacuum tubes replaced by semiconductor devices?
cards.definition: Tubes are bulky, power-hungry, need high voltages (~100 V), need a heated cathode, and have a short life. Semiconductor devices are small, low-power, low-voltage, long-lived, reliable

cards.term: In which direction do electrons flow in a vacuum diode? Why “valve”?
cards.definition: Only from cathode to anode, so the device acts like a one-way valve

cards.term: Where do the mobile charges in a semiconductor device come from?
cards.definition: From the solid itself (controlled by light, heat or a small voltage); no external heating or vacuum needed

cards.term: Early semiconductor detector of radio waves?
cards.definition: A crystal of galena (PbS) with a metal point contact

cards.term: Classify solids by resistivity ρ and conductivity σ.
cards.definition: Metals: ρ ~ 10⁻²–10⁻⁸ Ω m (σ ~ 10²–10⁸ S/m). Semiconductors: ρ ~ 10⁻⁵–10⁶ Ω m. Insulators: ρ ~ 10¹¹–10¹⁹ Ω m

cards.term: Types of semiconductors (with examples)?
cards.definition: Elemental: Si, Ge. Compound inorganic: GaAs, CdS, CdSe, InP. Organic: anthracene, doped phthalocyanines; polymers: polypyrrole, polyaniline

cards.term: Which semiconductors does the chapter study?
cards.definition: Inorganic Si and Ge (most devices are made of them)

cards.term: Valence band and conduction band?
cards.definition: Valence band: the energy band containing the valence electrons’ levels. Conduction band: the band above it; electrons here are free to move

cards.term: Why do energy bands form in a solid?
cards.definition: Outer orbits of neighbouring atoms overlap, so each electron sees a unique surrounding and gets a slightly different energy: closely spaced levels form bands

cards.term: Band structure of Si and Ge at 0 K?
cards.definition: The 8N states split into two bands with a gap E_g: the lower valence band (4N states) is completely full with the 4N valence electrons; the upper conduction band (4N states) is empty

cards.term: Correction: NCERT writes the outer electrons of Si/Ge as “2s and 2p”. What is right?
cards.definition: Slip: Si has 3s² 3p² and Ge 4s² 4p² (outermost orbit n = 3 and n = 4, as the same paragraph says)

cards.term: Energy band diagram of a metal?
cards.definition: Conduction and valence bands overlap (E_g ≈ 0) or the band is partially filled: many free electrons, high conductivity

cards.term: Energy band diagram of an insulator?
cards.definition: Large gap E_g > 3 eV: no electrons in the conduction band; thermal energy cannot bridge the gap

cards.term: Energy band diagram of a semiconductor?
cards.definition: Small gap E_g < 3 eV (0.2–3 eV): at room temperature a few electrons cross into the conduction band

cards.term: Band gaps of C (diamond), Si, Ge and Sn?
cards.definition: 5.4 eV, 1.1 eV, 0.7 eV (Ge 0.72), 0 eV (tin, a metal)

cards.term: Example 14.1: why is carbon an insulator while Si and Ge are semiconductors, with the same lattice?
cards.definition: Bonding electrons lie in shells n = 2, 3, 4: ionisation energy (E_g) is least for Ge, then Si, largest for C. So conduction electrons are significant for Ge, Si and negligible for C

cards.term: Teacher addition: how does resistance vary with temperature for a metal and a semiconductor?
cards.definition: Metal: R increases with T (more collisions). Semiconductor: R decreases with T (more electron–hole pairs); temperature coefficient of resistance is negative

cards.term: Teacher addition: is an insulator with a small E_g at high temperature a conductor?
cards.definition: Its conductivity rises with T; the classification depends on E_g relative to kT (≈ 0.026 eV at 300 K)

cards.term: Crystal structure of Si and Ge?
cards.definition: Diamond-like cubic structure: each atom has four nearest neighbours; lattice spacing C 3.56 Å, Si 5.43 Å, Ge 5.66 Å

cards.term: What is a covalent (valence) bond in Si?
cards.definition: Two atoms share electron pairs; each atom shares one of its four valence electrons with each of four neighbours

cards.term: Intrinsic semiconductor: definition?
cards.definition: A pure semiconductor whose carriers come only from thermal breaking of bonds; n_e = n_h = n_i

cards.term: What is a hole?
cards.definition: A vacancy in a covalent bond left when an electron breaks free; it behaves like a free particle with effective positive charge +q

cards.term: How does a hole “move”?
cards.definition: A neighbouring bound electron jumps into the vacancy, leaving a hole at its own site: the hole appears to move in the opposite direction to the electron

cards.term: Total current in an intrinsic semiconductor?
cards.definition: \( I = I_e + I_h \); holes move towards the negative potential (hole current in the direction of the field)

cards.term: Generation and recombination?
cards.definition: Thermal generation of electron–hole pairs is balanced at equilibrium by recombination (an electron falling into a hole)

cards.term: Intrinsic semiconductor at T = 0 K and at T > 0 K?
cards.definition: 0 K: behaves as an insulator (valence band full, conduction band empty). T > 0: thermally excited electrons partly occupy the conduction band, leaving equal holes

cards.term: Energy-band picture of an intrinsic semiconductor at T > 0 K?
cards.definition: Some electrons in the conduction band and an equal number of holes in the valence band

cards.term: Teacher addition: how does intrinsic carrier concentration n_i vary with temperature and gap?
cards.definition: n_i ∝ T^{3/2} e^{−E_g/2kT}: rises rapidly with temperature and falls for a larger gap (Si at 300 K: ~1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³)

cards.term: Teacher addition: mobility of electrons vs holes?
cards.definition: μ_e > μ_h (electrons move more freely than holes): σ = e(nₑμₑ + nₕμₕ)

cards.term: What is doping? What are extrinsic semiconductors?
cards.definition: Deliberate addition of a small amount (parts per million) of a suitable impurity (dopant) to a pure semiconductor to raise conductivity manifold: extrinsic (impurity) semiconductors

cards.term: Condition on the size of the dopant atom?
cards.definition: Its size must be nearly the same as that of Si/Ge so that it does not distort the lattice

cards.term: Dopants for Si and Ge?
cards.definition: Pentavalent (As, Sb, P): n-type. Trivalent (B, Al, In, Ga): p-type

cards.term: How does a pentavalent dopant make an n-type semiconductor?
cards.definition: Four of its five valence electrons form bonds; the fifth is very loosely bound (ionisation energy ~ 0.01 eV for Ge, 0.05 eV for Si) and is free at room temperature. The dopant is a donor

cards.term: Majority and minority carriers in n-type material?
cards.definition: Electrons are majority, holes minority (n_e ≫ n_h). The crystal stays electrically neutral

cards.term: How does a trivalent dopant make a p-type semiconductor?
cards.definition: It has one electron too few, leaving a vacancy (hole) in the fourth bond; a neighbour’s electron fills it and the hole moves on. The dopant is an acceptor (becomes a fixed negative ion)

cards.term: Majority and minority carriers in p-type material?
cards.definition: Holes are majority, electrons minority (n_h ≫ n_e); one acceptor gives one hole

cards.term: Mass-action law for doped semiconductors?
cards.definition: \( n_en_h = n_i^2 \) (in thermal equilibrium, in every case); doping raises one carrier type and reduces the other via recombination

cards.term: Why do the minority carriers decrease with doping?
cards.definition: The abundant majority carriers give the thermally generated minority carriers many more chances to recombine

cards.term: Energy-band picture of an n-type semiconductor?
cards.definition: A donor level E_D lies just below E_C (~ 0.01–0.05 eV); nearly all donors are ionised at room temperature, so most conduction electrons come from the dopant

cards.term: Energy-band picture of a p-type semiconductor?
cards.definition: An acceptor level E_A lies just above E_V (~ 0.01–0.05 eV); electrons jump up into it, leaving holes in the valence band

cards.term: Mnemonic: donor vs acceptor?
cards.definition: Donor → n-type (Negative carriers, pentavalent, 5 electrons: “Donate a Negative”). Acceptor → p-type (Positive holes, trivalent, 3 electrons: “Accepts electrons”)

cards.term: Do the number of donor electrons depend on temperature?
cards.definition: Weakly: donor electrons depend on doping level, not temperature, while the intrinsic pairs rise weakly with temperature

cards.term: Carrier densities in doped Si (Example 14.2)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 14.2 · doped silicon

Find the missing step.

Si crystal with 5 × 10²⁸ atoms/m³ is doped with 1 ppm arsenic. Find n_e and n_h (n_i = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³).
  1. N_D = 10⁻⁶ × 5 × 10²⁸ = 5 × 10²² m⁻³
  2. n_i ≪ N_D, so n_e ≈ N_D = 5 × 10²² m⁻³
  3. ?
  4. n_h ≈ 4.5 × 10⁹ m⁻³ (a factor 10¹³ smaller)
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 14.2 · doped silicon

Find the missing step.

Si crystal with 5 × 10²⁸ atoms/m³ is doped with 1 ppm arsenic. Find n_e and n_h (n_i = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³).
  1. N_D = 10⁻⁶ × 5 × 10²⁸ = 5 × 10²² m⁻³
  2. n_i ≪ N_D, so n_e ≈ N_D = 5 × 10²² m⁻³
  3. n_h = n_i²/n_e = (2.25 × 10³²)/(5 × 10²²)
  4. n_h ≈ 4.5 × 10⁹ m⁻³ (a factor 10¹³ smaller)

cards.term: Exercise 14.1: in n-type silicon which statement is true?
cards.definition: (c): holes are minority carriers and pentavalent atoms are the dopants

cards.term: Exercise 14.2: the true statement for p-type semiconductors?
cards.definition: (d): holes are the majority carriers and trivalent atoms are the dopants

cards.term: Exercise 14.3: carbon, silicon, germanium band gaps?
cards.definition: (c) (E_g)_C > (E_g)_Si > (E_g)_Ge

cards.term: Teacher addition: a Ge crystal doped with In, or Si with P. n-type or p-type?
cards.definition: In (Group III): p-type. P (Group V): n-type

cards.term: Teacher addition: n-type and p-type materials are separately electrically neutral. Why?
cards.definition: The extra carriers (electrons or holes) are balanced by the equal and opposite charge of the ionised dopant cores fixed in the lattice

cards.term: Teacher addition: conductivity of an extrinsic semiconductor?
cards.definition: \( \sigma = e(n_e\mu_e + n_h\mu_h) \approx e\,n_e\mu_e \) (n-type) or \( e\,n_h\mu_h \) (p-type)

cards.term: Why is the p-n junction important?
cards.definition: It is the basic building block of diodes, transistors and many other devices

cards.term: Diffusion at a p-n junction?
cards.definition: Due to the concentration gradient, holes diffuse p → n and electrons n → p: the diffusion current

cards.term: How is the depletion region formed?
cards.definition: Electrons leaving n leave immobile positive donor ions; holes leaving p leave immobile negative acceptor ions. This space-charge layer, free of mobile carriers, is the depletion region (~ 0.1 µm thick)

cards.term: Figure 14.10 · Formation of the p-n junction
Drift current at a p-n junction?
cards.definition: The junction field (from the positive n-side space charge to the negative p-side charge) sweeps electrons p → n and holes n → p: drift current, opposite to diffusion

cards.term: Equilibrium in a p-n junction?
cards.definition: Diffusion current = drift current: no net current, constant barrier potential V₀

cards.term: Barrier potential (built-in potential V₀)?
cards.definition: The potential difference across the junction that opposes further diffusion: n side positive relative to p. About 0.7 V for Si and 0.3 V for Ge

cards.term: Direction of the electric field in the depletion region?
cards.definition: From the positive ions on the n-side towards the negative ions on the p-side, i.e. n → p

cards.term: Example 14.3: can two slabs of p- and n-type semiconductors simply be pressed together?
cards.definition: No: surface roughness ≫ atomic spacing (2–3 Å), so there is no atomic-level contact: the junction acts as a discontinuity. The junction must be grown in a single crystal

cards.term: Teacher addition: as the depletion layer grows, why does diffusion stop?
cards.definition: The growing field raises the drift current and makes it equal the diffusion current; the barrier V₀ is set by the doping levels and temperature

cards.term: What is a semiconductor diode? Symbol?
cards.definition: A p-n junction with metallic contacts: a two-terminal device. The arrow head (from p to n) shows the conventional current direction in forward bias

cards.term: Forward bias: connections and effect on the barrier?
cards.definition: p to +, n to −. The applied field opposes V₀: the depletion layer narrows and barrier falls to \( V_0 - V \)

cards.term: Effect of forward bias on carriers?
cards.definition: Barrier reduced, more carriers cross: minority-carrier injection (electrons into p-side, holes into n-side); current is large (mA)

cards.term: Reverse bias: connections and effect on the barrier?
cards.definition: n to +, p to −. The applied field adds to V₀: the depletion layer widens and barrier rises to \( V_0 + V \)

cards.term: Why is the reverse current tiny and nearly voltage-independent?
cards.definition: It is due to minority carriers swept across (drift), limited by their concentration, not by the applied voltage; of the order of µA

cards.term: Depletion layer and barrier in bias
cards.definition: Forward bias narrows the depletion region and lowers the barrier to V0 − V giving a large current; reverse bias widens it and raises the barrier to V0 + V giving a tiny current

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
p-n junction · bias

How do the depletion layer, barrier height and current of a p-n junction change with no bias, forward bias and reverse bias?

Watch the width of the grey layer.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
p-n junction · bias

How do the depletion layer, barrier height and current of a p-n junction change with no bias, forward bias and reverse bias?

Forward bias (p to +, n to −): the applied voltage opposes V₀, so the depletion layer narrows, the barrier falls to V₀ − V and a large current (mA) flows by minority-carrier injection.

Reverse bias: the barrier rises to V₀ + V, the depletion layer widens, and only the tiny minority-carrier drift current (µA) flows: a one-way valve.

cards.term: Diode breakdown voltage?
cards.definition: At a critical reverse voltage V_br the reverse current increases sharply; an ordinary diode is destroyed if the current is not limited by the circuit

cards.term: Experimental set-up for diode characteristics?
cards.definition: Diode + potentiometer/rheostat + battery; a milliammeter in forward bias and a microammeter in reverse bias

cards.term: Typical V–I characteristic of a Si diode?
cards.definition: Forward: almost no current till the threshold (cut-in) voltage (~0.7 V Si, ~0.2 V Ge), then it rises exponentially. Reverse: tiny constant reverse saturation current till breakdown

cards.term: Threshold voltage of Si and Ge diodes?
cards.definition: ~0.7 V (Si) and ~0.2 V (Ge)

cards.term: Dynamic resistance of a diode?
cards.definition: \( r_d = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I} \): the small-signal ratio; low in forward bias, very large in reverse bias

cards.term: Forward and reverse resistance (Example 14.4)
cards.definition: r_fb = 10 Ω; r_rb = 1.0 × 10⁷ Ω

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 14.4 · diode resistance

Find the missing step.

For a silicon diode: (a) resistance at I_D = 15 mA (b) resistance at V_D = −10 V (reverse current 1 µA). Read: 0.7 V at 10 mA, 0.8 V at 20 mA.
  1. (a) Between 10 mA and 20 mA the curve is nearly a line: ΔV = 0.1 V, ΔI = 10 mA
  2. ?
  3. (b) At −10 V, I = −1 µA
  4. r_rb = 10 V/1 µA = 1.0 × 10⁷ Ω
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 14.4 · diode resistance

Find the missing step.

For a silicon diode: (a) resistance at I_D = 15 mA (b) resistance at V_D = −10 V (reverse current 1 µA). Read: 0.7 V at 10 mA, 0.8 V at 20 mA.
  1. (a) Between 10 mA and 20 mA the curve is nearly a line: ΔV = 0.1 V, ΔI = 10 mA
  2. r_fb = ΔV/ΔI = 0.1/(10 × 10⁻³) = 10 Ω
  3. (b) At −10 V, I = −1 µA
  4. r_rb = 10 V/1 µA = 1.0 × 10⁷ Ω

cards.term: Exercise 14.4: in an unbiased p-n junction holes diffuse from p to n because…?
cards.definition: (c) hole concentration is greater in the p-region than in the n-region (concentration gradient)

cards.term: Exercise 14.5: forward bias applied to a p-n junction…?
cards.definition: (c): lowers the potential barrier

cards.term: Teacher addition: ideal diode?
cards.definition: Zero resistance in forward bias (short circuit) and infinite resistance in reverse bias (open circuit); a practical Si diode has a 0.7 V drop when conducting

cards.term: Teacher addition: a diode in series with a resistor and a battery. Current?
cards.definition: If forward biased: I = (E − 0.7)/R for silicon (E − 0 for ideal); if reverse biased: I ≈ 0 (open circuit)

cards.term: Teacher addition: diode forward current equation?
cards.definition: \( I = I_0\left(e^{eV/kT} - 1\right) \) (Shockley): exponential in forward bias, saturates at −I₀ in reverse bias

cards.term: What is rectification?
cards.definition: Converting ac to a unidirectional (pulsating dc) voltage using the one-way conduction of a diode

cards.term: Half-wave rectifier: circuit and action?
cards.definition: Transformer secondary → diode in series with R_L. Output appears only in the half-cycles when the diode is forward biased

cards.term: Half-wave rectifier waveforms?
cards.definition: Output = positive half-cycles only; output frequency = input frequency (50 Hz)

cards.term: Full-wave rectifier: circuit and operation?
cards.definition: Two diodes with a centre-tap transformer: D₁ conducts in one half-cycle and D₂ in the other; both give current through R_L in the same direction (each diode rectifies half of the secondary voltage)

cards.term: Frequency of output of half-wave and full-wave rectifiers for 50 Hz input? (Exercise 14.6)
cards.definition: Half-wave: 50 Hz. Full-wave: 100 Hz

cards.term: Another full-wave circuit?
cards.definition: The bridge rectifier with four diodes needs no centre-tapped transformer

cards.term: Why is a filter needed after a rectifier?
cards.definition: The rectified output is pulsating (half sinusoids); a filter removes the ac ripple to give steady dc

cards.term: How does a capacitor filter work?
cards.definition: The capacitor across R_L charges to the peak, then discharges slowly through R_L (time constant R_LC) while the input dips, and is recharged in the next pulse; large C gives a smoother output

cards.term: Half-wave, full-wave and filtered output
cards.definition: Half-wave output has the input frequency and full-wave twice the input frequency; a capacitor filter smooths the pulses to nearly steady dc with time constant RLC

cards.term: Alternative filter?
cards.definition: An inductor in series with R_L (choke input filter)

cards.term: Why must the diode’s reverse breakdown voltage exceed the peak ac secondary voltage?
cards.definition: Otherwise the diode breaks down in the non-conducting half-cycle and is damaged

cards.term: Teacher addition: peak inverse voltage (PIV) for half-wave and centre-tap full-wave rectifiers?
cards.definition: Half-wave: PIV = V_m. Centre-tap full-wave: PIV = 2V_m (V_m = peak of half the secondary). Bridge: PIV = V_m

cards.term: Teacher addition: average (dc) and rms values of the output of half-wave and full-wave rectifiers?
cards.definition: Half-wave: V_dc = V_m/π, V_rms = V_m/2. Full-wave: V_dc = 2V_m/π, V_rms = V_m/√2

cards.term: Teacher addition: ripple factor and efficiency?
cards.definition: Half-wave: efficiency 40.6%, ripple factor 1.21. Full-wave: efficiency 81.2%, ripple factor 0.48

cards.term: Teacher addition: why does the capacitor filter output approach V_peak?
cards.definition: With large R_LC the discharge is small between recharge pulses, so the output stays close to the peak value of the rectified voltage

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: Zener diode?
cards.definition: A heavily doped p-n diode designed to operate in reverse breakdown; the voltage across it stays nearly constant (V_Z) over a wide current range. Used as a voltage regulator

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: how does a Zener regulator work?
cards.definition: Connect the Zener in reverse across the load with a series resistor R_s. If input voltage or load current changes, the extra current passes through the Zener while V_out = V_Z stays fixed; the difference is dropped across R_s

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: two breakdown mechanisms?
cards.definition: Zener breakdown (heavy doping, thin depletion layer, V_Z < 5 V: strong field pulls electrons from bonds) and avalanche breakdown (lighter doping, V > 6 V: impact ionisation)

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: light-emitting diode (LED)?
cards.definition: A forward-biased heavily doped p-n junction that emits light on electron–hole recombination; photon energy ≈ E_g. Made from GaAs, GaP, GaAsP; colour set by the gap (Si and Ge are useless as they are indirect)

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: photodiode?
cards.definition: A p-n junction operated in reverse bias; photons of energy hν ≥ E_g create electron–hole pairs and the reverse current rises with light intensity (light detector)

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: solar cell?
cards.definition:
A p-n junction (large area, no bias) that turns light into electricity by generating an emf across the junction; the I–V curve is in the fourth quadrant.
Materials: Si, GaAs, CdTe

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: modes of the three optoelectronic junctions?
cards.definition: LED: forward bias, emits light. Photodiode: reverse bias, detects light. Solar cell: no bias, generates power

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: the junction transistor?
cards.definition: A three-region device (n-p-n or p-n-p): emitter (heavily doped), base (thin, lightly doped), collector (moderately doped, larger). Emitter–base forward biased, collector–base reverse biased

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: transistor current relations?
cards.definition: \( I_E = I_B + I_C \); \( \alpha = \dfrac{I_C}{I_E} \) (< 1), \( \beta = \dfrac{I_C}{I_B} \) (50–200), \( \beta = \dfrac{\alpha}{1-\alpha} \)

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: a transistor as an amplifier (common emitter)?
cards.definition: A small change in base current gives a large change in collector current phase reversal of 180° between input and output voltage gain A_v = β R_L/R_i

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: a transistor as a switch?
cards.definition: In cut-off (base off) it is an open switch; in saturation (large base current) a closed switch

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: logic gates (digital electronics)?
cards.definition: Circuits that follow Boolean logic: OR, AND, NOT (basic) and NAND, NOR (universal gates) plus XOR

cards.term: Logic gates (NEET/JEE addition)
cards.definition: OR: Y = A + B; output 1 if any input is 1; AND: Y = A · B; output 1 only if both inputs are 1; NOT: Y = NOT A; inverts the input; NAND: Y = NOT(A · B); AND followed by NOT (output 0 only if both inputs are 1); NOR: Y = NOT(A + B); OR followed by NOT (output 1 only if both inputs are 0); XOR: Y = A ⊕ B; output 1 if inputs differ

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Logic gates

Boolean expression and output rule?

ORY = A + B; output 1 if any input is 1
ANDY = A · B; output 1 only if both inputs are 1
NOTY = NOT A; inverts the input
NANDY = NOT(A · B); AND followed by NOT (output 0 only if both inputs are 1)
NORY = NOT(A + B); OR followed by NOT (output 1 only if both inputs are 0)
XORY = A ⊕ B; output 1 if inputs differ

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: which gates are universal? Why?
cards.definition: NAND and NOR: any Boolean function (AND, OR, NOT) can be built from either alone

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: truth table of NAND for inputs (A, B) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)?
cards.definition: Outputs: 1, 1, 1, 0

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: truth table of NOR for the same inputs?
cards.definition: Outputs: 1, 0, 0, 0

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: NOT gate built from a NAND gate?
cards.definition: Join both inputs together: Y = NOT(A · A) = NOT A

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: symbols of gates?
cards.definition: AND: D-shaped OR: curved-back shield NOT: triangle with a bubble NAND/NOR: AND/OR with a bubble at the output

cards.term: Are E_C and E_V localised in space?
cards.definition: No: band energies are delocalised averages; drawn as straight lines they mean the bottom of the conduction band and the top of the valence band

cards.term: How can compound semiconductors become n- or p-type?
cards.definition: By changing the stoichiometric ratio (e.g. Ga-rich or As-rich GaAs) as well as by doping; defects control semiconductor properties

cards.term: NEET pattern: in a p-n junction diode, holes diffuse from p to n because…?
cards.definition: Of the concentration gradient (not because of an applied field)

cards.term: NEET pattern: the depletion layer in a p-n junction consists of…?
cards.definition: Immobile ionised donors and acceptors (no mobile carriers)

cards.term: NEET pattern: in forward bias the width of the depletion region and the barrier height?
cards.definition: Both decrease

cards.term: NEET pattern: electron–hole pairs in a pure Si crystal at T > 0 K: n_e vs n_h?
cards.definition: n_e = n_h = n_i; after n-type doping, n_e ≫ n_h but n_e n_h = n_i² still

cards.term: NEET pattern: Si doped with B. Nature and majority carriers?
cards.definition: p-type, holes

cards.term: NEET pattern: with a half-wave rectifier of 50 Hz input, ripple frequency?
cards.definition: 50 Hz (full-wave gives 100 Hz)

cards.term: JEE pattern: given the ratio n_e/n_h in a semiconductor, find the type and n_i.
cards.definition: n_e n_h = n_i²: e.g. n_e = 10²² and n_h = 10¹⁰ gives n_i = √(10³²) = 10¹⁶ m⁻³ and it is n-type

cards.term: JEE pattern: a diode with 0.7 V drop in series with 100 Ω across a 5.7 V battery, forward biased. Current?
cards.definition: I = (5.7 − 0.7)/100 = 50 mA

cards.term: JEE pattern: an ideal diode circuit: two diodes in parallel branches with different resistors, which conducts?
cards.definition: The diode whose anode is at the higher potential (forward biased) conducts; the other is reverse biased and acts as an open circuit

cards.term: Board pattern: differentiate between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors.
cards.definition:
Intrinsic: pure, n_e = n_h, conductivity small and strongly temperature-dependent.
Extrinsic: doped, n_e ≠ n_h, much higher conductivity from majority carriers

cards.term: Board pattern: differentiate n-type and p-type.
cards.definition: n-type: pentavalent donor, electrons majority, donor level just below E_C. p-type: trivalent acceptor, holes majority, acceptor level just above E_V

cards.term: Chapter 14 summary
cards.definition: Insulator band gap: E_g > 3 eV; Semiconductor band gap: E_g between 0.2 and 3 eV (Si 1.1, Ge 0.7); Metal: E_g ≈ 0 (bands overlap); Intrinsic: n_e = n_h = n_i; Mass action: n_e n_h = n_i²; n-type / p-type dopants: Pentavalent (donor) / trivalent (acceptor); Forward bias: p to +; barrier V₀ − V; mA current; Reverse bias: p to −; barrier V₀ + V; µA current; Cut-in voltage: 0.7 V (Si), 0.2 V (Ge); Rectifier output frequency: Half-wave f; full-wave 2f
